card.name: Fouetté
card.tagline: The 32-turn classical ballet feat of strength, stamina, and precision.
card.profile: The fouetté turn, or fouetté en tournant, is a brilliant classical ballet movement characterized by a whipping motion of the working leg that generates momentum for a 360-degree rotation. Originating in French terminology meaning 'whipped', it demands exceptional strength and balance as the dancer executes continuous turns on a single supporting foot. Its most famous incarnation is the execution of 32 consecutive fouettés, a bravura test introduced by Italian ballerina Pierina Legnani.
card.insight: First performed 32 times consecutively by Pierina Legnani in 1893, counting them became an obsessive pastime for St. Petersburg audiences.

card.profile_long: The fouetté turn, or fouetté en tournant, is a celebrated and highly demanding movement of classical ballet. Origins and History: The movement achieved legendary status on December 17, 1893, when Italian ballerina Pierina Legnani performed 32 consecutive fouettés during the premiere of the ballet Cinderella, choreographed by Lev Ivanov, Enrico Cecchetti, and Marius Petipa, with music by Baron Boris Vietinghoff-Scheel. Konstantin Skalkovski, the dance critic for the St. Petersburg Gazette, noted that Legnani performed the 32 turns without stopping and without traveling a single centimeter, turning the counting of the turns into an audience favorite. Legnani later repeated this feat as Odile in the Black Swan Pas de Deux of Swan Lake in 1895, cementing the 32 fouettés as a staple of classical repertoire. Other ballerinas, such as Mathilde Kschesinskaya and American prima ballerina Jeanne Devereaux—who held a record of 16 triple fouettés—further pushed the boundaries of this technical feat. How It Is Danced: A fouetté turn begins with the performer standing on one flat foot in plié with the knee bent. The working leg is extended and whipped around to the side to create the necessary angular momentum. Once extended to maximum turnout, the working leg is bent and pulled into a retiré or passé position, with the foot beating behind and then to the front of the supporting knee before extending back out. Simultaneously, the supporting foot transitions to relevé, rising to en pointe on toe tips in classical ballet. Music and Instruments: The music accompanying the historic introduction of the 32 fouettés in Cinderella was composed by Baron Boris Vietinghoff-Scheel, and the move is later integrated into grand pas sections of works like Swan Lake. Occasions and Meaning: Executing 32 consecutive fouettés is considered a supreme test of a ballerina's strength, stamina, and technique. It is notoriously difficult, with many dancers capable of performing the sequence on only one side, normally the right. Notable Figures: Pierina Legnani, Konstantin Skalkovski, Mathilde Kschesinskaya, and Jeanne Devereaux are central historical figures tied to the evolution and record-breaking execution of the movement. Lineage: As a core element of classical ballet, the fouetté stands as a pinnacle of technical mastery within the classical-court family of dance.

sections.origins_and_history: The fouetté en tournant was introduced in the Grand Pas d'azione of the ballet Cinderella on December 17, 1893, with choreography by Lev Ivanov, Enrico Cecchetti, and Marius Petipa, and music by Baron Boris Vietinghoff-Scheel. Pierina Legnani performed 32 consecutive fouettés without traveling, a feat reported by St. Petersburg Gazette critic Konstantin Skalkovski. Legnani repeated this in Swan Lake (1895), and Mathilde Kschesinskaya later achieved the same milestone.
sections.how_it_is_danced: A fouetté turn begins standing on one flat foot in plié with the knee bent. The working leg is extended and whipped to the side to create momentum, then pulled into a retiré or passé position while the supporting foot rises to relevé or en pointe. This creates the angular momentum needed for a rotation in place.
sections.music_and_instruments: The historic introduction of 32 consecutive fouettés in Cinderella featured music by Baron Boris Vietinghoff-Scheel. The movement is subsequently incorporated into the grand pas and major ballets such as Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performing 32 consecutive fouettés is considered a bravura demonstration of a ballerina's strength, stamina, and technique. It is a highly difficult feat that many dancers can execute on only one side, usually the right.

sections.regional_variants: Variants include petit fouetté (devant, à la seconde, derrière, executed à terre, sur la demi-pointe, or sauté) and grand fouetté (sauté, relevé, or en tournant).
sections.lineage: A foundational virtuoso step of classical ballet within the classical-court tradition.
